subject: Biology
title: Horizontal Gene Transfer
description: A quick win: understand Horizontal Gene Transfer.

hook.text: Bacteria don't need sex to swap genes. They can grab DNA from their neighbors—or even from dead cells.

buildup.text: Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) moves genes between unrelated organisms, bypassing parent-to-offspring inheritance.

discovery.text: Antibiotic resistance genes spread between bacterial species through HGT—jumping from harmless to deadly strains.

twist.text: About 8% of the human genome came from ancient viruses that inserted their DNA into our ancestors' cells.

climax.text: HGT means the tree of life is more like a web at the microbial level—branches fuse and swap.

punchline.text: You don't need parents to share genes. Just neighbors.

quiz.question: What percentage of the human genome came from ancient viruses?

details.summary: Horizontal gene transfer moves genetic material between organisms outside of parent-to-offspring inheritance. Common in bacteria through conjugation, transformation, and transduction, it enables rapid sharing of traits like antibiotic resistance across species boundaries.
details.whyItMatters: Horizontal gene transfer spreads antibiotic resistance between bacterial species at alarming speed, making it a critical public health concern. It also reveals that evolution is not always a branching tree but sometimes a tangled web.
takeaways: Bacteria share resistance genes through plasmid transfer between unrelated species
HGT makes the tree of life resemble a web among prokaryotes
About 8 percent of the human genome consists of ancient viral DNA insertions

faq.question: How do bacteria share genes horizontally?
faq.answer: Through conjugation, bacteria connect via a pilus and transfer plasmids. In transformation, bacteria absorb free DNA from the environment. In transduction, bacteriophage viruses accidentally package bacterial DNA and transfer it to new hosts.

faq.question: Does horizontal gene transfer occur in complex organisms?
faq.answer: Yes, though less frequently. About 8 percent of the human genome comes from ancient retroviral insertions. Some animals have acquired genes from bacteria and fungi. Parasitic plants transfer genes with hosts. It is far rarer than in bacteria but does occur.
